nt: ה֚וֹי הַ⁠שַּׁאֲנַנִּ֣ים בְּ⁠צִיּ֔וֹן וְ⁠הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֖ים בְּ⁠הַ֣ר שֹׁמְר֑וֹן

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Woe to the ones who feel completely secure in Zion and in Samaria]

Amos is using the word **Woe** to express a strong feeling of grief and to warn of coming disaster. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Great disaster will come upon]

Here, **the mountain of Samaria** refers to the fortified capital city that was built on that mountain, and so it represents the security that its leaders believed they had. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the defenses of the city of Samaria to keep them safe]

The implication of the phrase **the first of the nations** is that these leaders regarded Israel as the elite of all the nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the nation that they consider foremost among all nations]
The pronoun **them** refers to the complacent leaders in Zion and Samaria whom Amos has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to these leaders]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the nation of Israel]

x.ASV: Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines: are they better than these kingdoms? or is their border greater than your border?
x.Darby: Pass unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go to Hamath the great; and go down to Gath of the Philistines: are they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border?
x.KJV: Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: be they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border?
x.YLT: Pass ye over to Calneh and see, And go thence to Hamath the great, And go down to Gath of the Philistines, Are they better than these kingdoms? Greater is their border than your border?

nt: The kingdoms of Judah (represented by Zion) and Israel (represented by Samaria) are being compared to the kingdoms represented by the cities named in this verse. Because of the parallel structure of the two questions in this verse, it is most likely that **they** refers to the cities that have just been named, and that **these kingdoms** refers to Judah and Israel. Alternate translation: [Are those cities better than your kingdoms]
הֲ⁠טוֹבִים֙ מִן־הַ⁠מַּמְלָכ֣וֹת הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה אִם־רַ֥ב גְּבוּלָ֖⁠ם מִ⁠גְּבֻלְ⁠כֶֽם

The expected answer to these questions is “No.” The speaker is using the question form to emphasize that Judah and Israel are **better** in the sense that they are larger and more prosperous than the nations around them. It is possible that Amos is quoting these words from the “designated ones” who are boasting about their kingdoms. But since he refers to **your border**, it seems more likely that Amos is speaking to the “designated ones” and pointing out that, although God has made their kingdoms great, he will also destroy them because they are not better in the way that they should be. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as exclamations or as statements, as in the UST.

If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the second person throughout. Alternate translation: [you who put far off the evil day, but bring near]

This phrase resumes the description of the people whom Amos pronounced disaster or “woe” upon in [6:1](../06/01.md), and that description continues through verse 6. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to repeat the statement about the woe together with the information about these people and beginning a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [Woe to you! You put far off the evil day]

Amos is speaking of these people refusing to think about the coming day of judgment as if that day were an object that they were **putting far off**, or physically pushing away from themselves. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones pushing away the thought of the evil day] or [the ones refusing to think about the coming day of disaster]

Here, Amos is referring to “the day of Yahweh” mentioned in [5:18](../05/18.md) as **the evil day** since it was the time when Yahweh will bring justice by punishing them. Alternate translation: [the day of disaster that Yahweh will bring]

Here Amos is speaking hastening the coming time of violent rule as if that time were an object that could be **brought** physically **near**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you are hastening the arrival of a time of violence] or [but you are making the time when violent people will rule come sooner]

Here, **a seat of** represents “a throne” or “a reign of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a reign of violence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a violent rule]

nt: **Lo Debar** is the name of a town. It means, “not a thing.” So although this was a real town that Israel had captured, Amos is also saying that they are rejoicing over nothing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote.

These people are using the question form to boast about their own strength. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Indeed, by our own strength we have taken Karnaim for ourselves!]

**Karnaim** is the name of a town. It means, “a pair of horns,” which is a symbol of strength. Amos is implying that just as the strength of Karnaim did not help them, neither should Israel trust in their own strength. Only Yahweh is truly strong. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote.
